where: Section 1, opening of the bullet list (and exam trap 3)
problem: The sentence "Transformed matrices keep the same eigenvectors" is true in one direction only. Every eigenvector of A is an eigenvector of A⁻¹, A^k and p(A), but A^k and p(A) can have extra eigenvectors that A does not have. Example: A = [[0,1],[0,0]] has only one eigenvector line, while A² = 0 has every vector as an eigenvector. Trap 3 ("the eigenvectors stay the same") repeats the same overstatement.
fix: Say: "Every eigenvector of A is also an eigenvector of A⁻¹, A^k and p(A), with eigenvalue 1/λ, λ^k and p(λ). The transformed matrix may have extra eigenvectors, so its eigenspaces can be larger." Keep the warning "do not replace eigenvectors by powers".

problem: "Multiplicities then tell you how many independent eigenvectors are available" suggests the algebraic multiplicity gives the count. It does not: a(λ) only gives an upper bound, and the actual number g(λ) must be computed from null(A−λI).
fix: "Multiplicities bound the number of independent eigenvectors: 1 ≤ g(λ) ≤ a(λ), and checking equality g(λ)=a(λ) decides whether diagonalization is possible."

where: Section 3, proof that distinct eigenvalues give independent eigenvectors
problem: After applying A−λmI the shorter relation is c1(λ1−λm)v1+…+c(m−1)(λ(m−1)−λm)v(m−1)=0. The text does not say why this is a real contradiction: it is nontrivial because c_i ≠ 0 and λ_i ≠ λ_m, so every coefficient is nonzero.
fix: Add: "Each coefficient c_i(λ_i−λ_m) is nonzero, since the eigenvalues are distinct and c_i ≠ 0, so this is a shorter nontrivial relation. That contradicts the choice of a relation with the fewest nonzero coefficients."

where: Section 3, last sentence of the formula paragraph
problem: "Equality g(λ)=a(λ) for every eigenvalue is exactly the condition for diagonalizability" is incomplete for real matrices. A real rotation such as [[0,−1],[1,0]] has eigenvalues i, −i with g=a=1, yet it is not diagonalizable over the reals because it has no real eigenvectors.
fix: Say: "Equality g(λ)=a(λ) for every eigenvalue, together with the condition that all eigenvalues are real when the matrix is real and diagonalization is asked over R, is exactly the condition for diagonalizability." Or state that the criterion is over C.
